source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Krystal_1994_SubanestheticEffectsHumans.pdf, printed pp. 199-214 (16 PDF pages; PDF page N is printed page 198+N, confirmed from the running feet). Scanned pages with an error-prone text layer, so every number used was checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi: pp. 200, 203, 204, 205, 206, 207 and 209, including Figures 3 and 4 and the Methods sample and timing paragraphs.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement; the claim is if anything stricter than the paper, and rightly so. Three points. (1) The ceiling argument is correct and the figure bears it out: immediate recall sits at about 3.0 of 3 in every condition at every time, so F8,120 = 0.0 is uninformative. (2) 'In 18 volunteers given 40-minute infusions' is right for the behavioural measures but not for the cognitive ones: memory used 16, vigilance 14, verbal fluency 15 and the card-sorting comparison 19 (6, 5 and 8 on their first day). The claim's own magnitude says 'n = 14 to 18', which is the fairer range, though 19 took the card-sorting test. (3) The card-sorting sentence is exactly right: it was a between-person comparison of first test days, with no baseline, which the paper states (the test cannot be repeated once the rules are learned).
claims.note: Every Krystal number in the statement and magnitude checked on the rendered printed pages (scanned pages, error-prone text layer). p. 207: 10-min delayed recall dose x time F8,120 = 3.4, P = .002; immediate recall F8,120 = 0.0, P = NS; postdistraction F8,120 = 1.7, P = .1; memory n = 16. p. 206: verbal fluency n = 15, 16.1 +/- 1.3, 15.1 +/- 1.2, 12.9 +/- 1.3, dose F2,28 = 4.4, P = .02, high against placebo F1 = 8.4, P = .007 (printed with a single subscript, no error df); card sorting 6.5 +/- 0.8, 16.8 +/- 7.9, 31.9 +/- 7.0, F2,16 = 4.6, P = .03, n = 6, 5 and 8. p. 205: vigilance n = 14, 29.7 +/- 0.1, 29.6 +/- 0.2, 28.5 +/- 0.4, F2,26 = 8.6, P = .001; MMSE dose x time F8,136 = 1.4, P = .2, n = 18. All as printed, with one exception: the claim's magnitude gives word generation as 'SEM 1.3' etc., which is right (the paper prints mean +/- SEM). Editors' check of the vigilance magnitude: 29.7 - 28.5 = 1.2 of 30, so 'about one target of 30' is right. The card-sorting means cannot be reconciled with Figure 3 by eye (the plotted placebo bar sits near 9, the printed mean is 6.5); the bars may be medians, which the legend does not say.

anchors.locator: Subjects and Methods › Subjects; Ketamine Test Procedures › Ketamine Administration; Data Analysis
anchors.extracted: 19 healthy people recruited by advertisement, screened by structured interview and an informant interview, excluding psychiatric or substance use disorder, family history, or current life stress; urine toxicology at screening and on test days; 12 men (mean age 23.7, SEM 0.9) and 7 women (25.9, SEM 0.9). Three test days in randomized order: saline, ketamine hydrochloride 0.1 mg/kg and 0.5 mg/kg, each intravenously over 40 minutes (study conditions). One person withdrew after a first test day on the 0.5 mg/kg condition, leaving 18 for most analyses. Blood levels were not measured; the authors estimated plasma levels from published parameters (about 0.025-0.05 mg/L at the smaller condition and 0.1-0.25 mg/L at the larger). Frontal-lobe tasks began 20 min into the infusion and finished before it ended; the card-sorting test was analysed between people on first test days only, because it cannot be repeated.

anchors.locator: Results › Memory, 1st-2nd paragraphs (continues from p. 206); Figure 4
anchors.extracted: Three-word sets, recall tested immediately, after a distracting task and after a 10-minute delay, at five session times (n = 16). Overall: dose F2,30 = 60.6, delay F2,30 = 4.9 (P = .02), time F4,60 = 3.0 (P = .02), dose x time x delay F16,240 = 2.7 (P = .0006). Immediate recall dose x time F8,120 = 0.0 (not significant); postdistraction F8,120 = 1.7 (P = .1); 10-minute delayed recall F8,120 = 3.4 (P = .002), the fall marked at the 10-minute rating on the larger condition only. Figure 4 (read from the plot): immediate recall sits at about 3.0 of 3 in all conditions at all times; postdistraction falls to about 2.4 at the 10-minute rating on the larger condition; delayed recall falls from about 2.8 to about 1.2 at that rating and is back to about 2.5 by 80 minutes. On the larger condition, the fall in delayed recall did not correlate significantly with rises in positive symptoms (r = .2), negative symptoms (r = .07) or dissociation (r = .2).

anchors.locator: Results › Measures of Frontal Lobe Function › Verbal Fluency; Figure 3 (left panel)
anchors.extracted: Word generation in one minute (n = 15; 3 people excluded because their tests were not finished before the infusion ended): placebo 16.1 +/- 1.3 (SEM), smaller condition 15.1 +/- 1.2, larger 12.9 +/- 1.3; dose F2,28 = 4.4, P = .02; within-person post hoc contrast larger against placebo F1 = 8.4, P = .007; smaller against larger only a trend, F1 = 3.8, P = .06.

anchors.locator: Results › Measures of Frontal Lobe Function › Wisconsin Card Sorting Test; Figure 3 (right panel)
anchors.extracted: First test day only, between people: placebo n = 6, 0.1 mg/kg n = 5, 0.5 mg/kg n = 8 (19 in all). Perseverative errors 6.5 +/- 0.8, 16.8 +/- 7.9, 31.9 +/- 7.0; dose F2,16 = 4.6, P = .03; post hoc, the larger condition differed from placebo. Trials to first category 13.5 +/- 1.9, 14.6 +/- 2.5, 35.1 +/- 7.8 (F2,16 = 4.6, P = .03); total errors 12.8 +/- 2.2, 25.6 +/- 10.0, 53.4 +/- 8.4 (F2,16 = 8.0, P = .004); percent perseverative error 54 +/- 5, 62 +/- 5, 58 +/- 4 (F2,16 = 0.7, not significant); all completed six categories; correct items and losses of set did not differ. No pre-drug baseline exists for this test, and the standard errors at the two ketamine conditions are large relative to the means.

anchors.locator: Results › Measures of Frontal Lobe Function › Vigilance
anchors.extracted: Continuous performance test (n = 14; the test was added after 4 people had entered the study): items correctly identified 29.7 +/- 0.1, 29.6 +/- 0.2, 28.5 +/- 0.4 (dose F2,26 = 8.6, P = .001), i.e. about 1.2 of 30 fewer at the larger condition; omissions 0.3, 0.4, 1.5 (F2,26 = 8.6, P = .001); commissions 0.1, 0.2, 0.6 (F2,26 = 4.3, P = .03); reaction time unchanged (0.48, 0.46, 0.51 s; F2,24 = 1.8, P = .2).

No significant effect on the Mini-Mental State Examination (n = 18): dose x time F8,136 = 1.4, P = .2; peak decrease from baseline 0.7 +/- 0.4 (placebo), 0.2 +/- 0.1 and 0.3 +/- 0.2, dose F2,34 = 1.6, P = .2.

claims.overstatement: None. Two small things for the editor. (1) The CADSS figure given in the magnitude (F6,96 = 46.0, n = 17) is from the text; Figure 2's legend says n = 18 for the same scale, and the degrees of freedom match 17, so the text is right and the legend wrong. (2) 'Describe what was rated as hallucinatory behaviour as distortions of real stimuli rather than hallucinations' is a fair paraphrase of the paper's statement that hallucinatory behaviour was limited to illusory experiences in all sensory domains, but the same page also reports ideas of reference with paranoid content and formal thought disorder at the larger condition, so the sentence should not be read as saying nothing psychosis-like occurred.
claims.note: Checked on the rendered pages: p. 203 four key positive symptoms n = 18, dose F2,34 = 72.0, time F4,68 = 19.3, dose x time F8,136 = 22.9, all P = .0001, rises from baseline at the 10- and 80-minute ratings on the larger condition only (Dunnett t5,136 = 9.4 and 12.8, P < .01), scores back at baseline generally within 15 minutes of the end of the infusion. p. 204: three key negative symptoms dose x time F8,136 = 18.0. p. 205: CADSS total n = 17, dose F2,32 = 65.0, dose x time F6,96 = 46.0. p. 205: Perceptual Aberration n = 18, dose F2,34 = 35.4, dose x time F6,102 = 20.0, rises at 10 and 80 minutes on the larger condition only, also back at baseline generally within 15 minutes. p. 209: 8 of 18 (44%, four men and four women) had blurred vision on the larger-condition day, about half of those with horizontal nystagmus, and two women vomited. All as printed and all matching the claim.

anchors.locator: Results › BPRS Scores › Positive Symptoms of Schizophrenia; Figure 1 (left panel)
anchors.extracted: Four key BPRS items (conceptual disorganization, hallucinatory behaviour, suspiciousness, unusual thought content) in 18 people: dose F2,34 = 72.0, time F4,68 = 19.3, dose x time F8,136 = 22.9, all P = .0001; no baseline differences between test days; neither placebo nor the smaller condition changed scores; the larger condition raised scores from baseline at the 10- and 80-minute ratings (t5,136 = 9.4 and 12.8, P < .01), still significant after adjusting for the placebo day; scores returned to baseline generally within 15 minutes of the end of the infusion. Each of the four items rose separately (all dose x time P < .0001). Hallucinatory behaviour was limited to illusory experiences in all sensory domains; ideas of reference with paranoid content and formal thought disorder (loosening of association, derailment, stilted speech) were noted at the larger condition. No pretest measure of vulnerability to psychosis correlated with the placebo-corrected peak rise (r < .25).

anchors.locator: Results › BPRS Scores › Negative Symptoms of Schizophrenia; Figure 1 (right panel)
anchors.extracted: Three key BPRS items (blunted affect, emotional withdrawal, motor retardation), n = 18: dose F2,34 = 34.6, time F4,68 = 28.0, dose x time F8,136 = 18.0, all P = .0001; placebo produced no rise at any rating; the smaller condition raised scores only at the 80-minute rating (t5,136 = 2.56, P < .05); the larger condition raised them at 10 and 80 minutes (t5,136 = 9.1 and 12.6, P < .01), still significant after adjusting for the placebo day. Each of the three items rose separately (P < .0001).

anchors.locator: Results › Perceptual Alterations › Clinician-Administered Dissociative States Scale; Figure 2 (right panel)
anchors.extracted: CADSS total, n = 17 in the text (Figure 2's legend says 18; the degrees of freedom fit 17): dose F2,32 = 65.0, time F3,48 = 46.8, dose x time F6,96 = 46.0, all P = .0001; placebo produced no rise; the smaller condition gave a non-significant rise at 80 minutes (t4,96 = 2.56, P < .1); the larger condition raised scores at 10 and 80 minutes (t4,96 = 9.4 and 18.8, P < .01), still significant against the placebo day. All five subscales (body perception, environmental perception, feelings of unreality, memory impairment, time perception) showed dose and interaction effects, P = .0001; the subscales were sorted by the authors on face validity.

anchors.locator: Results › Perceptual Alterations › Perceptual Aberration Subscale; Figure 2 (left panel)
anchors.extracted: Self-rated perceptual change, n = 18: dose F2,34 = 35.4, time F3,51 = 26.7, dose x time F6,102 = 20.0, all P = .0001; no baseline differences; placebo and the smaller condition produced no change; the larger condition raised scores at 10 and 80 minutes (t4,102 = 12.9 and 18.7, P < .01), still significant against the placebo day; scores returned to baseline generally within 15 minutes of the end of the infusion. Peak rises on the clinician-rated and self-rated scales were not significantly correlated with each other on the larger-condition day.

8 of the 18 (44%; four men and four women) reported blurred vision on the larger-condition day, with horizontal nystagmus in about half of those cases; participants felt able to do tasks needing vision. Two women vomited on a larger-condition day, both with blurred vision and nystagmus at the time.

anchors.locator: Subjects and Methods › Behavioral Ratings; Ketamine Test Procedures
anchors.extracted: Randomized order of the three test days; BPRS and clinician-rated visual analogue scales at 30 and 15 minutes before, 10 minutes into the infusion, and 40, 70 and 190 minutes after its end; the Perceptual Aberration Subscale and the CADSS at the -30-, 10-, 80- and 110-minute points, so the latest perceptual rating was 70 minutes after the end of the infusion. Participants were told beforehand what ketamine might do, to reduce distress. The paper reports no blinding check anywhere. Blood levels were not measured.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high agreed. Two domains are rated 'high' where RoB 2 would more usually give 'some concerns' for probable unblinding without documented deviations, but the reasoning is sound for a study whose primary outcomes are clinician ratings in a condition with visible signs in 44% of participants, and the overall judgment is unaffected. The card is right that the card-sorting analysis is outside the within-person design; a per-outcome note that it is a between-person comparison would make that plainer in the domain table.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. The abstract's 'sparing immediate recall and postdistraction recall' rests on a three-word task at ceiling, and 'impaired performance on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test' rests on 6, 5 and 8 unmatched people on their first day with no baseline; both are presented in the abstract without those qualifications.

missed: The authors reviewed with each participant beforehand what ketamine might do, to reduce distress during the test day (Methods, p. 200). That is good practice but it also primes expectancy in a study with no blinding check, and it belongs beside the blinding domain.

The sample sentence on p. 200 says twelve men and seven women 'completed' the testing (19) while the next sentence says one withdrew after a first test day and the analyses use 18; this is a plain internal inconsistency in the completer count, slightly broader than reporting issue 6, which covers the sexes of the completers.

The within-person correlations that bear on whether the memory effect is separate from the symptom effects (KF 7, r = .2, .07, .2 at n = 16) are printed without signs, so even their direction is uncertain; the card notes the missing signs under reporting issue 2 but the consequence for that particular null result could be stated.
